title: Properties of Logarithms & Solving Exponential/Logarithmic Equations
learningObjective: EL5: Use properties of logarithms to condense or expand logarithmic expressions. EL6: Solve exponential and logarithmic equations.

faqs.question: What is the one-to-one property of logarithms, and why does it work?
faqs.answer:
The one-to-one property says that if two logarithms with the SAME base are equal, then their arguments must be equal too: \( \log_b(M) = \log_b(N) \) if and only if \( M = N \). This works because a logarithmic function is one-to-one (FN6) — each output comes from exactly one input — so if two logs with the same base produce the same output, they had to start from the same input.
Example

If \( \log_3(x) = \log_3(7) \), then \( x=7 \).

faqs.question: What is the product property of logarithms, and where does it come from?
faqs.answer:
The product property turns the logarithm of a product into a sum of two separate logarithms.
Formula

\[ \log_a(m \cdot n) = \log_a(m) + \log_a(n) \]

This comes directly from the exponent rule \( b^x \cdot b^y = b^{x+y} \) — since logarithms ARE exponents (EL3), multiplying two numbers corresponds to adding their exponents, which is exactly what this property captures.

faqs.question: What is the quotient property of logarithms?
faqs.answer:
The quotient property turns the logarithm of a fraction into a difference of two separate logarithms — the mirror image of the product property.
Formula

\[ \log_a\left(\dfrac{m}{n}\right) = \log_a(m) - \log_a(n) \]

faqs.question: What is the power property of logarithms?
faqs.answer:
The power property lets you move an exponent from inside a logarithm's argument out in front, as a multiplier.
Formula

\[ \log_a(m^n) = n \cdot \log_a(m) \]

This is one of the most useful properties for solving equations, since it's the tool that lets you "bring down" an exponent you're trying to solve for.

faqs.question: What is the change of base formula, and when would I need it?
faqs.answer:
The change of base formula rewrites a logarithm with any base as a ratio of two logarithms in a DIFFERENT, more convenient base — usually base 10 or base e, since those are the only two bases most calculators have a dedicated button for.
Formula

\[ \log_a(x) = \dfrac{\log_b(x)}{\log_b(a)} \]

(b can be any valid base — commonly 10 or e)

faqs.question: What does it mean to "expand" versus "condense" a logarithmic expression?
faqs.answer: Expanding means breaking one logarithm containing a product, quotient, or exponent into several simpler logarithms added or subtracted together. Condensing means running that process backward — combining several separate logarithms into a single logarithm. They're opposite skills using the exact same three properties (product, quotient, power), just applied in opposite directions.

faqs.question: How do I expand a logarithmic expression using the product, quotient, and power properties?
faqs.answer:
Work from the outside in: identify the overall structure first (is the whole thing a product, a quotient, or something raised to a power?), apply the matching property to split it into pieces, then repeat on any pieces that still have more than one factor.
Worked Example

Expand \( \log_2\left(\dfrac{x^3 y}{z}\right) \).

Quotient property: \( \log_2(x^3y) - \log_2(z) \)

Product property: \( \log_2(x^3) + \log_2(y) - \log_2(z) \)

Power property: \( 3\log_2(x) + \log_2(y) - \log_2(z) \)

faqs.question: How do I condense multiple logarithms into a single logarithm?
faqs.answer:
Run the expanding process in reverse: handle any coefficients in front of a logarithm first by moving them back up as exponents (power property backward), then combine addition into a product and subtraction into a quotient.
Worked Example

Condense \( 2\log(x) + \log(y) - \log(z) \).

Power property backward: \( \log(x^2) + \log(y) - \log(z) \)

Product then quotient: \( \log\left(\dfrac{x^2y}{z}\right) \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation when both sides already have the same base?
faqs.answer:
Use the one-to-one property of exponentials: if the bases match, you can simply set the exponents equal to each other and solve — no logarithms needed at all.
Worked Example

Solve \( 5^{3x} = 5^{7x-2} \).

Same base, so set exponents equal: \( 3x = 7x-2 \)

Solve: \( -4x=-2 \) → \( x=\dfrac{1}{2} \)

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation when the two sides have different bases?
faqs.answer: First check whether you can rewrite both sides using a common base (like rewriting 4 as 2²) — if so, use the one-to-one property from faq-9. If the bases genuinely can't be matched, take the logarithm of both sides instead (faq-11).

faqs.question: How do I solve an exponential equation using the "take the log of both sides" method?
faqs.answer:
Take log (or ln) of both sides, use the power property to bring the exponent down as a multiplier, then solve the resulting equation algebraically for the variable.
Worked Example

Solve \( 3^x = 7 \).

Take log of both sides: \( \log(3^x) = \log(7) \)

Power property: \( x\log(3) = \log(7) \)

Solve: \( x = \dfrac{\log(7)}{\log(3)} \approx 1.771 \)

faqs.question: How do I solve a logarithmic equation by condensing it into a single logarithm first?
faqs.answer:
Condense the equation into the form \( \log_b(\text{something}) = \text{a number} \), then convert to exponential form (EL3) and solve algebraically.
Worked Example

Solve \( \log_2(x) + \log_2(x-2) = 3 \).

Condense: \( \log_2(x(x-2)) = 3 \)

Convert to exponential form: \( x(x-2) = 2^3 = 8 \)

Solve the resulting quadratic: \( x^2-2x-8=0 \) → \( x=4 \) or \( x=-2 \)

faqs.question: How do I check for extraneous solutions when solving a logarithmic equation?
faqs.answer:
Plug every candidate solution back into the ORIGINAL equation (before you condensed or converted anything) and confirm every logarithm's argument comes out positive. Since a logarithm's domain requires a positive argument (EL3), any solution that makes an argument zero or negative must be thrown out — even though it solved the condensed algebraic equation correctly.
Worked Example

From faq-12: candidates \( x=4 \) and \( x=-2 \).

Check \( x=-2 \) in the original: \( \log_2(-2) \) — argument is negative, undefined.

Reject \( x=-2 \). Only \( x=4 \) is a valid solution.

faqs.question: How do I use the change of base formula to evaluate a logarithm on a calculator?
faqs.answer:
Rewrite the logarithm as a fraction of two common (or natural) logarithms using the change of base formula (faq-5), then evaluate each one on a calculator and divide.
Worked Example

Evaluate \( \log_5(30) \).

Change of base: \( \dfrac{\log(30)}{\log(5)} \)

\( \approx \dfrac{1.477}{0.699} \approx 2.113 \)

faqs.question: How do the properties of logarithms in EL5 make solving equations possible in EL6?
faqs.answer: EL5's properties are the actual tools EL6 puts to work. The power property is what lets you bring a trapped exponent down to solve for it. The product and quotient properties are what let you condense a multi-term logarithmic equation into the single \( \log_b(\text{something}) = \text{number} \) form you need before converting to exponential form and solving. Without EL5's toolkit, none of EL6's equation-solving methods would be possible.

faqs.question: How does this section connect back to EL1–EL4?
faqs.answer: Every piece of this section leans on something earlier in the unit. EL1 and EL3 gave you the exponential and logarithmic definitions these properties are built from. EL2 and EL4's domain and asymptote rules are exactly why you have to check for extraneous solutions (faq-13) — a candidate solution isn't valid unless it actually lands inside the function's domain. This section is less a brand-new topic and more the payoff of everything the unit has been building toward.

faqs.question: Why do these equation-solving skills matter beyond this course?
faqs.answer: Solving exponential and logarithmic equations is the essential skill behind answering real questions like "how long until this investment doubles," "how long until this radioactive sample decays to half its original amount," or "how many years until a population reaches a certain size." Anywhere a real-world exponential model shows up, eventually you need to solve for the input — and that's exactly the skill this section builds.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL5 leans on: exponent rules and logs as exponents (EL3). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Exponent rules
stops.target: Use the three exponent rules: \(b^m b^n = b^{m+n}\), \(\dfrac{b^m}{b^n} = b^{m-n}\), \((b^m)^p = b^{mp}\). Also move factors with negative exponents across the fraction bar: \(y^{-5} = \dfrac{1}{y^5}\).
stops.cold: Simplify (a) \(x^3 \cdot x^4\) (b) \(\dfrac{x^7}{x^2}\) (c) \((x^3)^4\). Then (d) write \(x^3 y^{-5}\) as a fraction with positive exponents.
stops.coldPlain: Simplify (a) x^3 * x^4, (b) x^7/x^2, (c) (x^3)^4. Then (d) write x^3 y^(-5) as a fraction with positive exponents.
stops.solution: Multiplying powers of the same base adds exponents; dividing subtracts; a power of a power multiplies. A negative exponent means the factor belongs in the denominator: y^(-5) = 1/y^5.
stops.mistake: Multiplying exponents in (a) or dividing them in (b).
stops.again: Write \(\dfrac{n^6}{m^2 k^3}\) as a product with no fraction bar, using negative exponents.
stops.reflect: Which operation on powers turns into addition of exponents?

stops.title: Logs of powers
stops.target: Remember from EL3: a log is an exponent, so \(\log_b(b^k) = k\).
stops.cold: Evaluate \(\log_2(2^5)\), \(\log_2 8\), and \(\log_2 4\). What do you notice about \(\log_2(8 \cdot 4)\)?
stops.coldPlain: Evaluate log_2(2^5), log_2 8, and log_2 4. What do you notice about log_2(8 * 4)?
stops.coldA: \(5\), \(3\), \(2\). And \(\log_2(8 \cdot 4) = \log_2 32 = 5 = 3 + 2\): the log of a product is the sum of the logs. That pattern is the next stop.
stops.solution: log_2(2^5) = 5 because the log is the exponent. log_2 8 = 3 and log_2 4 = 2. 8 * 4 = 32 = 2^5, so log_2(32) = 5 = 3 + 2. Multiplying inside became adding outside, because 2^3 * 2^2 = 2^(3+2).
stops.againA: \(4\), \(2\), and \(\log_3 9 = 2 = 4 - 2\). Dividing inside became subtracting outside.
stops.reflect: Why would multiplying inside a log turn into adding outside it?

stages.desc: The three properties and where they come from, then expanding and condensing (the EL5 check), common mistakes, and change of base.

stops.title: Product and quotient rules
stops.target: \(\log_b(MN) = \log_b M + \log_b N\) and \(\log_b\left(\dfrac{M}{N}\right) = \log_b M - \log_b N\). A log is an exponent, so the exponent rules become log rules.
stops.explain:
Where the properties come from

Each log property is an exponent rule in disguise, because a log is an exponent.

[[graph:RULES]]
stops.coldA: \(\log_3 x + \log_3 y\) (product rule) and \(\log_3 x - \log_3 y\) (quotient rule).
stops.solution: A product inside becomes a sum of logs (product rule). A quotient inside becomes a difference: numerator minus denominator (quotient rule).
stops.mistake: Writing log_3(x/y) as log_3 x / log_3 y.
stops.reflect: Which exponent rule is the product rule really using?

stops.title: Power rule
stops.target: \(\log_b(M^p) = p\log_b M\): an exponent inside the log moves to the front as a coefficient.
stops.coldA: \(5\log_2 x\) and \(-3\log_7 y\). Negative exponents come out as negative coefficients.
stops.solution: The power rule moves the exponent to the front: log_2(x^5) = 5 log_2 x; log_7(y^(-3)) = -3 log_7 y.
stops.mistake: Writing (log_2 x)^5, which is a different thing.
stops.reflect: What is the difference between \(\log(x^5)\) and \((\log x)^5\)?

stops.title: Expand step by step
stops.target: Expand one log into sums and differences, one property per step, and name the property each time: quotient, then product, then power.
stops.cold: Expand \(\log_4\left(\dfrac{x^3 z^2}{y^5}\right)\), naming the property at each step.
stops.coldPlain: Expand log_4( x^3 z^2 / y^5 ), naming the property at each step.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: Step 1, quotient rule: log_4(x^3 z^2) - log_4(y^5). Step 2, product rule: log_4(x^3) + log_4(z^2) - log_4(y^5). Step 3, power rule: 3 log_4 x + 2 log_4 z - 5 log_4 y.
stops.mistake: Applying the power rule to the whole fraction, or dropping the minus sign in front of the denominator term.
stops.again: Expand \(\log_6\left(a^{-2} b^4 c^{-7}\right)\), naming each property. (This is the form the CheckIt uses.)
stops.againA: Final answer: \(-2\log_6 a + 4\log_6 b - 7\log_6 c\). With negative exponents you only need the product and power rules.[[graph:EX2]]
stops.reflect: Why does the quotient rule usually come first when expanding?

stops.title: Condense step by step
stops.target: Condense a sum and difference of logs into one log by running the properties backward: power first (coefficients become exponents), then product and quotient.
stops.cold: Condense \(3\log_5 a - 4\log_5 b + 2\log_5 c\), naming the property at each step.
stops.coldPlain: Condense 3 log_5 a - 4 log_5 b + 2 log_5 c, naming the property at each step.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: Step 1, power rule backward: log_5(a^3) - log_5(b^4) + log_5(c^2). Step 2, product rule: log_5(a^3 c^2) - log_5(b^4). Step 3, quotient rule: log_5(a^3 c^2 / b^4).
stops.mistake: Combining before moving the coefficients up, which leaves a 3 or 4 stranded outside the log.
stops.reflect: Why must the coefficients move up first?

stops.title: Common mistakes
stops.target: The properties only work for products, quotients, and powers inside one log. \(\log(x + y)\) cannot be split, and \(\dfrac{\log x}{\log y}\) is not \(\log\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\).
stops.cold:
True or false? Test each with \(x = 10\), \(y = 100\) and base-10 logs.
(a) \(\log(x + y) = \log x + \log y\) (b) \(\log(xy) = \log x + \log y\) (c) \(\dfrac{\log x}{\log y} = \log\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)\) (d) \((\log x)^2 = 2\log x\)
stops.coldPlain: True or false, testing with x = 10, y = 100, base-10 logs: (a) log(x + y) = log x + log y; (b) log(xy) = log x + log y; (c) log x / log y = log(x/y); (d) (log x)^2 = 2 log x.
stops.coldA: (a) False: \(\log 110 \approx 2.04\), but \(1 + 2 = 3\). (b) True: \(\log 1000 = 3 = 1 + 2\). (c) False: \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) vs. \(\log 0.1 = -1\). (d) False: \((\log 10)^2 = 1\), but \(2\log 10 = 2\). The power rule is \(\log(x^2) = 2\log x\), with the exponent inside.
stops.solution: (a) log 110 is about 2.04, not 3, so false: there is no rule for a sum inside a log. (b) True, the product rule. (c) log 10 / log 100 = 1/2, but log(0.1) = -1, so false. (d) (log 10)^2 = 1 but 2 log 10 = 2, so false: the power rule needs the exponent inside the log, log(x^2) = 2 log x.
stops.mistake: Splitting log(x + y) into log x + log y.
stops.again: Can \(\log_3(9 + 27)\) be simplified with a log property? Can \(\log_3(9 \cdot 27)\)?
stops.againA: \(\log_3(9 + 27) = \log_3 36\): no property applies to a sum. \(\log_3(9 \cdot 27) = \log_3 9 + \log_3 27 = 2 + 3 = 5\).
stops.reflect: What is the quickest way to test whether a "rule" you remember is real?

stops.title: Change of base
stops.target: \(\log_b a = \dfrac{\ln a}{\ln b} = \dfrac{\log a}{\log b}\). Use it to evaluate any log on a calculator.
stops.explain:
Why change of base works

Let \(c = \log_3 20\). That means \(3^c = 20\). Take \(\ln\) of both sides: \(\ln(3^c) = \ln 20\). The power rule gives \(c \ln 3 = \ln 20\), so \(c = \dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 3}\). The same steps work for any base.
stops.cold: Use change of base to evaluate \(\log_3 20\) to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: Use change of base to evaluate log_3 20 to four decimal places.
stops.solution: log_3 20 = ln 20 / ln 3, about 2.7268. It makes sense: 3^2 = 9 and 3^3 = 27, so the answer must be between 2 and 3.
stops.mistake: Dividing in the wrong order (ln 3 / ln 20), or computing ln(20/3).
stops.again: Evaluate \(\log_7 50\) to four decimal places. Estimate first.
stops.againA: \(7^2 = 49\), so it should be just over 2. \(\dfrac{\ln 50}{\ln 7} \approx 2.0104\).
stops.stretch: Rewrite \(y = \log_2 x\) so you could type it into a calculator that only has \(\ln\).
stops.reflect: How can you estimate a log before using change of base, to check your answer?

stages.desc: A practice check in the EL5 CheckIt format (expand and condense, naming each property), plus change of base.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Expand and condense logarithmic expressions step by step, naming each property, and use change of base.
stops.cold:
(1) Demonstrate step-by-step how to expand \(\log_7\left(m^4 w^{-3} s^2\right)\), explaining the property used at each step.
(2) Demonstrate step-by-step how to condense \(5\log_2 k - 2\log_2 t + 3\log_2 n\), explaining each step.
(3) Evaluate \(\log_4 30\) to four decimal places.
stops.coldPlain: (1) Expand log_7( m^4 w^(-3) s^2 ) step by step, naming each property. (2) Condense 5 log_2 k - 2 log_2 t + 3 log_2 n step by step. (3) Evaluate log_4 30 to four decimal places.
stops.note: Show every step and name the log property (product, quotient, or power rule) you used at each step. Check that I named the right property each time.
stops.solution: (1) Product rule: log_7(m^4) + log_7(w^-3) + log_7(s^2); power rule: 4 log_7 m - 3 log_7 w + 2 log_7 s. (2) Power rule backward: log_2(k^5) - log_2(t^2) + log_2(n^3); product: log_2(k^5 n^3) - log_2(t^2); quotient: log_2(k^5 n^3 / t^2). (3) ln 30 / ln 4 is about 2.4534 (between 2 and 3, since 4^2 = 16 and 4^3 = 64).
stops.mistake: Not naming the property at each step; the check asks for it.
stops.again:
(1) Expand \(\log_8\left(d^{-6} x^5 a^{-2}\right)\), naming each property.
(2) Condense \(-3\log_6 y + 7\log_6 z - 4\log_6 b\), naming each property.
(3) Evaluate \(\log_9 2\) to four decimal places.
stops.againA: (1) \(-6\log_8 d + 5\log_8 x - 2\log_8 a\)[[graph:F2a]](2) \(\log_6\left(\dfrac{z^7}{y^3 b^4}\right)\)[[graph:F2b]](3) \(\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 9} \approx 0.3155\) (less than 1, since 2 is less than 9)
stops.reflect: Which direction (expanding or condensing) is harder for you, and which property trips you up?

paths.label: EL6: Solving Exponential and Log Equations
paths.sectionLabel: EL6, Solving Exponential and Logarithmic Equations
paths.intro: Builds to the EL6 check: solving exponential and logarithmic equations, plus same-base equations, taking ln of both sides, and checking for extraneous solutions.

stages.desc: Two quick reviews EL6 leans on: converting forms (EL3) and condensing (EL5). Skip any you already have.

stops.title: Switch between log and exponential form
stops.target: Recall from EL3: \(b^c = a\) and \(\log_b a = c\) say the same thing.
stops.cold: Rewrite \(2^x = 7\) in log form, and \(\log_3 x = 4\) in exponential form.
stops.coldPlain: Rewrite 2^x = 7 in log form, and log_3 x = 4 in exponential form.
stops.solution: 2^x = 7: base 2, exponent x, result 7, so x = log_2 7. log_3 x = 4: base 3, exponent 4, so x = 3^4 = 81.
stops.mistake: Writing x = log_7 2 (swapping base and result).
stops.reflect: Converting is what "undoes" an exponent or a log. Why is that useful for solving?

stops.title: Condense logs
stops.target: Recall from EL5: combine \(\log_b M + \log_b N\) into \(\log_b(MN)\) and \(\log_b M - \log_b N\) into \(\log_b\left(\tfrac{M}{N}\right)\).
stops.solution: Product rule: a sum of logs with the same base is the log of the product: log_2(x(x - 2)).
stops.reflect: Why would you want an equation to have only one log in it?

stages.desc: Exponential equations first, then log equations. The big habit: isolate the power or the log, then convert.

stops.title: Same base on both sides
stops.target: If both sides can be written as powers of the same base, set the exponents equal: \(b^m = b^n\) means \(m = n\).
stops.solution: Write 8 as 2^3, then match exponents: x + 1 = 3, x = 2. For 9^x = 27, rewrite both with base 3: 3^(2x) = 3^3, so 2x = 3 and x = 3/2.
stops.reflect: When does the same-base method not work?

stops.title: Exponential equations: isolate, then convert
stops.target: When the bases cannot match, get the power alone, then rewrite in log form. Give the exact answer as a log, then a decimal with change of base.
stops.cold: Solve \(3^{x - 4} = 7\) and \(2^x - 5 = 9\). Give exact answers and decimals.
stops.coldPlain: Solve 3^(x - 4) = 7 and 2^x - 5 = 9. Give exact answers and decimals.
stops.coldA: [[graph:S1]]The graph shows the same answer: the curve \(y = 3^{x-4}\) meets the line \(y = 7\) at \(x \approx 5.77\).[[graph:I1]][[graph:S2]]
stops.solution: 3^(x - 4) = 7: the power is alone, so x - 4 = log_3 7, x = log_3 7 + 4, about 5.7712. 2^x - 5 = 9: add 5 first, 2^x = 14, so x = log_2 14, about 3.8074.
stops.mistake: Taking the log before isolating, like writing x = log_2 9 + 5 for 2^x - 5 = 9.
stops.reflect: Why must the power be alone before you convert?

stops.title: Take ln of both sides
stops.target: Another route: take \(\ln\) of both sides and use the power rule to bring the exponent down. This is the go-to move for base \(e\) and for different bases on each side.
stops.solution: ln(3^x) = ln 20 becomes x ln 3 = ln 20 by the power rule, so x = ln 20 / ln 3 (the same as log_3 20). For e^(2x) = 9: ln(e^(2x)) = 2x, so 2x = ln 9 and x = ln 9 / 2.
stops.reflect: How is taking ln of both sides the same as using change of base?

stops.title: Log equations: isolate, then convert
stops.target: Get the log alone, rewrite in exponential form, solve, and check that the argument is positive.
stops.solution: 4 log_2(3x) = 12: divide by 4, log_2(3x) = 3, so 3x = 2^3 = 8 and x = 8/3. 5 + log_3(2y) = 7: subtract 5, log_3(2y) = 2, so 2y = 9 and y = 9/2. Both arguments are positive.
stops.reflect: What is the same about the first move in exponential and log equations?

stops.title: Combine logs and check for extraneous solutions
stops.target: With more than one log, condense first (EL5), convert, solve, and then check every answer: any answer that puts a non-positive number inside a log is extraneous.
stops.coldA: Only \(x = 4\) works.[[graph:S5]]The graph agrees: the left side only exists for \(x > 2\), so it crosses \(y = 3\) once, at \(x = 4\).[[graph:I5]]
stops.solution: Condense: log_2(x(x - 2)) = 3. Convert: x(x - 2) = 8, so x^2 - 2x - 8 = 0, (x - 4)(x + 2) = 0. x = -2 makes log_2(-2) undefined, so reject it. x = 4: log_2 4 + log_2 2 = 3, correct.
stops.mistake: Keeping both answers without checking the domain.
stops.reflect: Why can solving correctly still produce an answer that does not work?

stages.desc: A practice check in the same four-equation format as the EL6 CheckIt exercise.

stops.title: Practice check
stops.target: Solve two exponential and two logarithmic equations, giving exact answers.
stops.cold:
Solve each equation for the variable. Give exact answers.
(a) \(2^{w - 5} = 9\) (b) \(3^n - 4 = 6\) (c) \(7\log_5(2a) = 14\) (d) \(3 + \log_4(5d) = 6\)
stops.coldPlain: Solve each equation, giving exact answers: (a) 2^(w - 5) = 9, (b) 3^n - 4 = 6, (c) 7 log_5(2a) = 14, (d) 3 + log_4(5d) = 6.
stops.reflect: What is your first move on every one of these equations?
